expected_evidence: Ice-core geochemistry: iridium and/or platinum concentration spike at the ~12.8 ka BP (~10,850 BCE) horizon in Greenland ice cores (e.g., GISP2, NGRIP), synchronous with a sharp temperature/methane inflection marking Younger Dryas onset
Associated ice-core or proximal sediment markers of biomass burning: elevated ammonium, black carbon/soot, and charcoal peaks coincident with the iridium/platinum layer
Magnetic and glassy microspherules or nanodiamonds in the same ice-core interval or in correlative terrestrial 'black mat' sediments across North America/Europe

Continental 'black mat' stratigraphic layers at archaeological and paleontological sites dated to the same interval, showing elevated Ir/Pt, soot, and charcoal consistent with continent-scale biomass burning ('impact winter' signature)
Megafaunal extinction and/or Clovis-culture discontinuity horizons stratigraphically coincident with the anomaly layer (indirect corroborating evidence of ecological disruption)

Independent replication of the iridium/platinum anomaly across multiple, geographically dispersed ice cores and sediment cores (needed to distinguish a true cosmic-impact signal from local contamination or non-impact volcanic/terrestrial sources)
Astronomical/orbital modeling or identification of a plausible impactor/fragmenting comet consistent with a synchronous, geographically broad delivery of platinum-group elements
response.rationale: The interval -10850 sits at the Younger Dryas onset boundary, so I treat this as a 'younger-dryas' period case (geological 0.65, astronomical 0.7, material 0.35, genetic 0.3, oral_tradition/iconographic 0.1, textual 0.0, model_prior 0.3). Greenland ice sheets are one of the best-preserving archives available for this era: they offer continuous, annually-to-sub-annually resolved stratigraphy over the required ~12,800 years, with well-established geochemical dating (layer counting, tie-points to other records), making detection of a real iridium/platinum anomaly and coincident biomass-burning proxies (ammonium, black carbon) highly plausible if the event occurred as described — consistent with the high geological/astronomical detectability scores in the table. However, corroborating this specific hypothesis (an actual cosmic impact causing an 'impact winter') requires more than a single anomaly: it needs replication across independent cores/sites and exclusion of alternative sources (volcanism, in-situ contamination), which raises the bar. Complementary terrestrial evidence (microspherules, nanodiamonds, black mats, megafaunal/Clovis discontinuities) is material-type evidence with much lower baseline detectability (0.35) due to poor organic/inorganic preservation over 13,000 years outside ice and select sedimentary contexts. Model-prior (unverified, from training, tier: model-prior): I recall that a real-world 'Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis' (Firestone et al. 2007; Petaev et al. 2013 platinum anomaly in GISP2) exists and has been actively debated, with several independent groups failing to replicate the anomaly at other sites and attributing signals to non-impact causes — this is contested, not settled, science, and I flag it explicitly as an unverified recollection rather than established fact. Given the strong ice-core preservation potential but the genuinely contested/mixed empirical record for this specific corroboration claim, I set the detectability adjustment at 0.55 — near the geological baseline but tempered to reflect that 'corroborated' status demands replicated, unambiguous cross-site evidence that the real record has struggled to deliver, meaning absence or weakness of confirming evidence should not be read as strong evidence of falsity, but as consistent with a still-debated, partially detectable signal.
